final_answer: No. The trial court most likely did not err (the disqualification should be upheld, reviewed for abuse of discretion). Under Texas law, a nonlawyer such as a legal assistant who switches sides is governed by the Phoenix Founders / American Home Products / Columbia Valley framework, which uses two presumptions. (1) Where the nonlawyer worked on the same matter for the former firm, she is conclusively (irrebuttably) presumed to have acquired the former client's confidences. Jones worked on Apex's case for two years, prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications and attended strategy meetings, so this presumption applies. Her claimed lack of recall is immaterial. (2) The second presumption, that she shared those confidences with the new firm, is ordinarily rebuttable by showing that the new firm took effective, timely steps to screen her (written policies, notice to the nonlawyer to avoid the case, no access to files, no discussion). But under Columbia Valley (Tex. 2010), the presumption of sharing becomes irrebuttable, and disqualification of the new firm is mandatory, where the nonlawyer actually worked on the same matter for the new firm (at least where the firm did not prevent that work and had not given her prior instruction). Here Jones worked on the Apex-Prestige dispute thirteen times over 2017-2022 as a substitute secretary and e-filed two documents in March 2022 under her own name for the firm's attorney. Smith Fullingham made no inquiry at hiring and imposed no screen until January 2023, after the work was done, so the screen was untimely and could not cure the problem. That the work was limited or secretarial, and that she says she disclosed nothing, does not help, because the rule does not ask whether actual disclosure occurred once the nonlawyer has worked on the matter for the new firm. The firm's lack of knowledge also does not excuse it, since the firm has the responsibility to ask about prior work and screen from hire (Tex. Disciplinary R. Prof'l Conduct 5.03 supervisory duty). Waiver/delay is the best counterargument: Texas courts hold that a party who unreasonably delays seeking disqualification may waive it (Vaughan v. Walther, 875 S.W.2d 690 (Tex. 1994); In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998)). It fails because Apex moved about two months after first learning of Jones's involvement in January 2023. Prestige, not Apex, would have to show unreasonable delay, and Apex had no earlier notice that she was working for the opposing firm (her name had not surfaced before March 2022 e-filing, and the firm never disclosed her). Disqualification is a severe remedy, and courts require the movant to show actual prejudice rather than mere allegations, but the Court treats the irrebuttable presumptions as satisfying that showing. Caveat: I could not retrieve the full text of the opinions within the budget (one fetch was blocked), so the precise wording of Columbia Valley's holding and the second-presumption rule should be confirmed against the opinion.
